title: The Firebrands of Hindu College
subtitle: A Young Poet Lights a Storm in Calcutta’s Classrooms
region: Entally, Hindu College and Calcutta's debating societies
moral: A small circle can still light difficult questions.

sources.citation: Henry Derozio, Poems (Calcutta, 1827) and The Fakeer of Jungheera (1828)
Academic Association records and Calcutta press notices, 1828-1831
sources.note: Contemporary evidence for Young Bengal debating culture and controversy.

sources.citation: Rosinka Chaudhuri, Gentlemen Poets in Colonial Bengal (2002); Supriya Chaudhuri, ODNB entry on Derozio (2009)

panels.shot: dramatic mid-shot in dim classroom, low angle

dialogue.text: In Calcutta, 1820s, a twenty-year-old Anglo-Indian poet, Henry Louis Vivian Derozio, turns Hindu College into a storm of questions that will cost him his post before cholera ends his life at twenty-two.

panels.shot: wide establishing shot of Calcutta streets

dialogue.text: Calcutta, 1809. In a city ruled by the Company, where English, Persian and Bengali mix in the dust, an Anglo-Indian boy named Henry Derozio grows up watching two worlds that seldom speak as equals.

panels.shot: intimate mid-shot in modest home interior

dialogue.text: Born in Calcutta to an Anglo-Portuguese Christian family, Henry lives at the edge of British privilege and Indian exclusion, teaching himself verse and history while most boys his age dream only of clerkships.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Henry reading and writing

dialogue.text: By his late teens, he has already poured his restlessness into poems, soon to be printed in Calcutta, and into a longer tale, The Fakeer of Jungheera, where love, faith and freedom collide on the page.

panels.shot: wide shot of Hindu College exterior, daytime

dialogue.text: In May 1826, Hindu College, founded by Bengali elites to teach Western learning, appoints the eighteen-year-old poet as teacher of English and history. Few expect the quiet youth to unsettle much.

But soon his classes become something new. Instead of rote recitation, he urges his Hindu College pupils to question, compare, argue, turning lessons into fierce discussions that stretch beyond the bell.

panels.shot: medium shot focusing on Henry and one student

dialogue.text: Do not repeat, think. Why should any practice stand above reason?
He speaks of liberty and rights, of reason and conscience, tying European ideas to the lives of young men bound by caste, family and a colonial state that keeps power to itself.

panels.shot: wide shot of evening gathering in classroom

dialogue.text: By 1828, these after-class talks harden into a circle. With Derozio’s urging, the boys form the Academic Association, a small society where they debate caste, women’s status, press freedom and rational religion.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a small hall, debating scene

dialogue.text: Academic Association records and press notices show fiery evenings. Young Bengal attacks rigid caste rules, calls for female education, and insists that religious claims must face the test of argument.

panels.shot: tense mid-shot in a modest dining room

dialogue.text: Some pupils go further. To prove caste can be broken, they publicly eat forbidden foods, drink wine, invite scandal. In an age of purity rules, each transgression echoes loudly through their families’ courtyards.

panels.shot: wide shot of Calcutta bazaar with gossiping elders

dialogue.text: The movement remains tiny, confined to an urban elite circle. Yet its noise is enough. Word spreads that a Christian Anglo-Indian at Hindu College is turning sons against customs and elders.

panels.shot: mid-shot of Hindu College corridor with administrators

dialogue.text: College authorities face pressure from guardians alarmed by reports of irreverence and taboo-breaking. Between a colonial administration and a conservative patronage, Derozio’s open questioning begins to look dangerous.
In April 1831, the tension breaks. Under conservative pressure, Hindu College dismisses Henry Derozio. The same institution that gave him a platform now shuts its doors, fearing his influence.

panels.shot: emotional mid-shot of Henry leaving college gate

dialogue.text: Keep asking. A dismissal cannot dismiss truth.

For Hindu College, it is an act of control. For his pupils, it is a shock: their mentor, barely past twenty, has been removed, leaving them to decide whether his questions survive outside the classroom.

panels.shot: intimate interior mid-shot of Henry at home, unwell

dialogue.text: That same year, cholera stalks Calcutta’s crowded lanes. In December 1831, the disease reaches Derozio. There is no hero’s battlefield, only ordinary sickness in an epidemic city, and a poet weakened at twenty-two.

panels.shot: quiet wide shot of his room with students visiting

dialogue.text: He dies on December 26, 1831. The city does not stop. Ships still move on the Hooghly, debates continue in other halls. His direct circle is small, yet those who sat in his classes carry a different fire now.

panels.shot: reflective montage-style wide shot of Calcutta debates

dialogue.text: Young Bengal never becomes a mass movement. Yet in the decades that follow, echoes of their questions appear in reformist writings, in campaigns for education and rights, and in the growing culture of public debate.

panels.shot: close-up of Henry’s poetry manuscript on table

dialogue.text: His writings remain: poems from 1827, a romantic tale from 1828, fragments of a mind convinced that reason and imagination belong in Calcutta’s classrooms as much as in London’s.

panels.shot: contemplative wide shot of an empty Hindu College classroom

dialogue.text: Henry Louis Vivian Derozio does not lead a nation; he reshapes a room. A tiny circle of students learns that even from a single classroom, hard questions can travel far beyond the walls that first feared them.
